prompt: Sort each queue item into its triage tier based on the signals given.

items.text: 98% confidence, wellness visit, 1 page, no flags
55% confidence, ED visit, 3 pages, no flags
88% confidence, follow-up, 2 pages, no flags
97% confidence, follow-up, 1 page, compliance flag fired

hints: A fired flag settles the tier before you even look at confidence.
Very high confidence with no flags and a short, low-risk note is the textbook fast-pass profile.
explanation: The rule runs in this order: a fired flag means Tier 3 regardless of confidence, because it caught something structural a confidence score doesn't measure. Without a flag, low confidence (roughly below 75%) on a longer or higher-risk note means Tier 3. High confidence, short note, low-risk encounter type, no flag means Tier 1. Everything else defaults to Tier 2 — which is most of a real queue, on purpose, since Tier 2 is where flat, unremarkable review time belongs.

prompt: A 99%-confidence, 5-page inpatient discharge summary has no fired flags. A colleague argues it should be Tier 1 because of the confidence score alone. Explain what's wrong with using confidence as the sole deciding signal here, and what tier you'd actually assign.
hints: Note length and encounter type both carry information confidence doesn't.
Discharge summaries routinely involve a principal-diagnosis decision among several documented comorbidities.
explanation: Confidence measures how closely the note's language matches patterns the pipeline associates with the proposed code — it says nothing about whether the encounter itself is inherently complex. A 5-page inpatient discharge routinely involves multiple comorbidities and a genuine judgment call about which condition is the principal diagnosis, a decision type that a confidence score doesn't evaluate at all. The right call is at minimum Tier 2, and arguably Tier 3 for a reviewer without deep fluency in discharge summaries specifically — note length and encounter-type risk override a comfortable confidence number here, the same way a fired flag would.

prompt: Put the three things a genuine two-minute review checks in the order they're described in this lesson.

items: Nothing in the note contradicts the proposed code
The proposed code matches the stated reason for the visit
An obviously-stated second condition got its own code

hints: The first check is the most structural one — does the code even match why the visit happened.
The contradiction check comes right after matching the stated reason.
explanation: The lesson names these in order: first, does the proposed code match the stated reason for the visit (a structural check); second, does anything in the note contradict the code (a scan for internal inconsistency); third, is an obviously-stated second condition also coded. All three are fast because they're pattern checks on a short note, not deep specificity judgments — which is exactly why specificity and cross-visit history checking don't make this list.

prompt: A reviewer's Tier 1 review time has dropped steadily over months while her small monthly audit keeps passing clean. What should she actually conclude?

options.text: Her review is genuinely fine — the audit proves it
A passing small sample doesn't rule out a shortcut that only fails on rarer cases
She should ask for a bigger Tier 1 queue to prove her speed

hints: A small random sample is disproportionately full of the easy cases that would pass even a shortcut.
The audit tests whether her calls were correct, not whether she actually ran the checks.
explanation: A passing small audit sample is not evidence a fast pass is real — it's only evidence the sample hasn't yet included one of the less-obvious cases the shortcut was never equipped to catch. The honest response is to check whether she can still name the three specific things a genuine fast pass checks, not to treat the clean audit as reassurance.

prompt: Match each batching action to what it's actually accomplishing.

pairs.left: Scanning the queue for specialty and encounter type before opening anything
pairs.right: Building clusters before spending any review time

pairs.left: Working a cardiology cluster start to finish before switching
pairs.right: Banking the context-loading saving instead of paying the switch cost anyway

pairs.left: Running triage tiers inside each cluster
pairs.right: Deciding how much time each item gets, separate from what order it's worked in

right: A different, unrelated batching-adjacent action, as a distractor.
Fixing a compliance flag on an item

hints: Batching and triage are solving two different costs — order versus time allocation.
The saving from batching only banks if you actually finish the cluster before switching context.
explanation: Scanning first builds the clusters before any review time is spent, so the sort itself is cheap. Finishing a cluster before switching is what actually banks the context-loading saving — a half-finished cluster followed by a different specialty pays the switch cost with nothing gained. And triage still runs inside each cluster because batching (order) and triage (time allocation) are answering different questions and don't substitute for each other.

prompt: Batching a queue by specialty label is sufficient on its own — any two items sharing a specialty label can always be worked back to back with no extra check.

config.statement: Batching a queue by specialty label is sufficient on its own — any two items sharing a specialty label can always be worked back to back with no extra check.
config.rubric: A correct justification names a case where the label is true but the actual context differs (workers' comp versus routine within the same specialty, a fired flag, unusual legal exposure) and explains that the specialty label describes clinical domain, not stakes or documentation standard.

hints: Think about a workers'-comp claim and a routine visit that both say the same specialty.
What does a compliance flag tell you that the specialty label doesn't?
explanation: False. The specialty label is a good default sort key, but it only describes clinical domain — it says nothing about documentation standard, payer stakes, or legal exposure. A workers'-comp orthopedics claim and a routine post-op check both labeled 'orthopedics' need genuinely different review modes. The skill is re-scanning each cluster for items that share the label but not the actual context, and pulling those out on their own.

prompt: Which of these is a reliable, behavior-based fatigue signal, per this lesson?

options.text: It's after 2pm
You notice you've stopped checking for secondary conditions on Tier 1 items
You've hit exactly 100 items today

hints: Clock time and item counts don't account for how today's fatigue curve differs from a typical day.
Which signal is about a behavior actually changing, not a number on a clock?
explanation: Skipping a check you'd normally run without thinking about it is a direct behavioral marker that comprehension and attention are already costing more effort than they did earlier — exactly the kind of shortcut the two-minute-review lesson warned about, here triggered by fatigue rather than backlog pressure. Clock time and fixed item counts are unreliable because the same person's fatigue curve shifts day to day with sleep and queue difficulty.

prompt: A supervisor-set daily item limit, chosen in advance, is enough on its own to protect a reviewer's accuracy across the whole shift.

config.statement: A supervisor-set daily item limit, chosen in advance, is enough on its own to protect a reviewer's accuracy across the whole shift.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that a limit set in advance can't see the live information (sleep, queue difficulty, breaks) that actually drives fatigue on a given day, so it can only set a coarse outer bound, not replace a signal-based rule inside it.

hints: What information is available when a supervisor sets a limit versus when a reviewer is actually working?
Think about a flare day versus a good day at the same item count.
explanation: False. A limit set in advance uses only information available before the day starts — it can't know whether today's fatigue arrives at item 90 or item 200. It's reasonable as a coarse outer bound for planning and staffing, but the signal-based rule (behavioral markers noticed during the day) is what actually protects accuracy, because it's the only mechanism that can see the live variable driving the errors.

prompt: Order these four ramp-up actions for a reviewer returning after several days out.

items: Return to normal pace and triage rhythm
Check for procedural changes that happened while away
Work a reduced-pace mixed batch for the rest of day one
Start with a small batch of Tier 1 items

hints: Nothing after the first step is trustworthy until you know what changed.
Tier 1 items are the low-stakes place to re-sync recognition before anything harder.
explanation: Checking for procedural changes comes first because every later step depends on knowing what's different — reviewing confidently is worthless if a payer rule changed underneath you. A small Tier 1 batch re-syncs recognition at low stakes next, then a reduced-pace mixed batch for the rest of day one, before returning to full normal pace on day two.

prompt: A colleague says the fifteen-minute check for procedural changes after time away is 'just a courtesy — it shows you're being conscientious.' Explain what's actually wrong with that framing.
hints: Careful, conscientious work recovers some kinds of gaps on its own over time — does it recover this one?
explanation: The framing misses what the check actually does. Careful, attentive review recovers speed and pattern-recognition gaps on its own over the first day back — those erode with time away and rebuild with practice. A procedural change (a new compliance flag type, an updated payer rule) is different in kind: it's information the reviewer simply doesn't have, and no amount of care or attentiveness substitutes for information you don't possess. Treating the check as a courtesy rather than a necessity is exactly how it gets skipped on a busy day, at which point a real gap goes uncaught rather than just unperformed.

prompt: A queue item shows 40% confidence, wellness visit, 1 page, no flags. Assign a tier and justify it in one sentence.
hints: Low confidence on an otherwise unremarkable note is itself worth noticing.
explanation: Tier 3, briefly. Low confidence on a short, routine-looking note is a real signal, not noise to ignore just because the other columns look easy — it can mean the note was unusually terse or documented something atypical for the visit type, and a quick full read resolves that faster than guessing.

prompt: Which pair of items batches together most sensibly?

options.text: A routine dermatology check and a routine cardiology follow-up, because both are Tier 2
Two cardiology follow-ups with similar note length and no flags
A workers'-comp orthopedics claim and a routine orthopedics post-op check, because both say orthopedics

hints: Batching groups by shared review context, not by shared tier.
A shared specialty label isn't the same as shared documentation stakes.
explanation: Two cardiology follow-ups genuinely share vocabulary, comorbidity patterns, and review mode — a real batching win. Sharing a tier doesn't mean sharing context (a Tier 2 dermatology check and a Tier 2 cardiology follow-up still cost a full context switch). And sharing a specialty label doesn't guarantee shared context either, as the workers'-comp case shows directly.

prompt: Order these four fatigue-response actions from earliest-appropriate to latest-appropriate across a session.

items: Continue normal pace, no signals present yet
Notice one fatigue signal (a re-read), keep working but stay alert
Notice two signals in the same hour, plan to stop soon
Stop for the day

hints: This mirrors the module's signal-based stopping rule, escalating with evidence.
explanation: The module's stopping rule is signal-based and escalates with evidence, not a single trigger: normal pace continues absent any signal; one isolated signal (a re-read) is worth noting but not yet acting on; two signals converging in the same hour is the point to plan a stop; and stopping happens once that threshold is reached, regardless of item count or clock time.

prompt: A reviewer who stops at a fixed 150 items every day, regardless of how the day felt, has a stopping rule that protects her accuracy as well as a signal-based rule would.

config.statement: A reviewer who stops at a fixed 150 items every day, regardless of how the day felt, has a stopping rule that protects her accuracy as well as a signal-based rule would.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that fatigue depends on information (sleep, queue difficulty, breaks taken) only available during the day, which a number fixed in advance can't see or respond to.

hints: What information does a fixed number, set before the day starts, have access to?
Compare a flare day to a good day at the same item count.
explanation: False. A fixed count is set using information available before the day starts; fatigue is driven by information only available during the day. On a day fatigue arrives early, 150 items has already cost far more than usual by the time it's reached; on a good day, it may end the shift with real capacity left unused. A rule that can't see the live variable can't respond to it.

prompt: You're back after five days out. Before opening your first chart, name two specific things you'd check, and why neither is something 'working carefully' can substitute for.
hints: One should be procedural (something that changed), one should be about your own recognition speed.
explanation: A strong answer names checking for procedural changes (new compliance flag types, updated payer rules, team announcements) and starting with a small Tier 1 batch to re-sync pattern recognition at low stakes. Neither substitutes for careful work: a procedural change is invisible information you simply don't have yet, no amount of care recovers it, only checking does. Recognition speed does recover with careful work over time, but starting at low stakes (Tier 1) means the recovery period doesn't also carry high-stakes risk.

prompt: A colleague says: 'I always review in the order the queue arrives — it's the fairest way to work through it.' What's the strongest response, using this module's terms?

options.text: Queue arrival order tracks clinic scheduling, not review difficulty, so 'fair' order still misallocates attention
Arrival order is fine as long as you work fast enough
Fairness isn't a relevant consideration for a review queue

hints: What actually determines the order items arrive in a queue?
Fairness to whom, exactly — the items, or the clinicians who closed them?
explanation: Arrival order reflects when clinicians closed their notes — a scheduling coincidence, not a measure of review difficulty. Working strictly in that order means your best attention goes wherever the schedule happened to put it, not where the queue actually needs it. Triage isn't unfair to items; it's the thing that makes attention allocation track difficulty instead of arrival time.

prompt: Item 172 today, and you catch yourself re-reading a straightforward note for the second time. Name the specific decision this module says you should make, and why 'push through, it's almost done' is the wrong instinct here.
hints: The signal is arriving well before any dashboard would confirm a problem.
explanation: The specific decision: this is one fatigue signal — worth noting, and combined with a second signal in the same window, worth planning to stop. 'Push through' treats the remaining queue as the only cost, ignoring that fatigue-driven errors on the remaining items are the actual, larger cost — the signal is arriving specifically because it predicts the next thirty items will be worse than the last thirty, not because the queue is almost empty.

prompt: A shop switches from counting only reimbursement-impacting errors to counting every deviation from the correct code set. What happens to reported accuracy, for identical underlying work?

options.text: It stays the same — errors are errors
It drops, because more things now count in the numerator
It rises, because more scrutiny catches more good calls too

hints: Think about what's now being counted that wasn't before.
The numerator (error count) is what changed here, not the underlying work.
explanation: Reported accuracy drops, because the numerator now includes reimbursement-neutral deviations that the old standard ignored entirely. Nothing about the coder's actual work changed — only the counting rule did. This is exactly why comparing accuracy numbers across shops (or across a job change) without checking the error-counting standard is comparing two different measurements as if they were one.

prompt: A supervisor wants to use a single aggregate accuracy number to decide which of two coders, working genuinely different case mixes, gets a bonus. Explain what's wrong with this plan using this lesson's terms, and suggest one better approach.
hints: What did the lesson say an aggregate accuracy number is and isn't good for?
explanation: An aggregate accuracy rate is a fair comparison only between matched formulas and matched case mixes — the lesson names this directly as one of the things a single number can't honestly support (ranking across different work). Using it to rank two coders on different case mixes bakes a structural difficulty difference into what looks like a skill comparison. A better approach: track each coder's own trend against their own consistent formula, or build case-mix-adjusted comparisons if a cross-person comparison is truly needed — not a raw side-by-side of two different denominators.

prompt: Sort each corrected claim by whether it fits a recurring pattern or looks like an isolated one-off, based on the coder's last ten corrections (described in the module).

items.text: Missed secondary diagnosis in a note where it's mentioned once, briefly (this is the 6th time this month)
Wrong place-of-service code on a telehealth claim with unusual documentation (first time seen)
Missed secondary diagnosis, brief mention, longer primary narrative (7th time)
Typo in a modifier code, caught and fixed immediately (never seen before)

hints: Count how many times the same shape shows up.
A pattern needs to recur to count as a targetable cluster, not just look similar once.
explanation: A pattern worth building a targeted fix around shows up multiple times with the same underlying shape — here, missing a briefly-mentioned secondary diagnosis, six or seven times. A one-off error, even a real one, doesn't yet justify a specific new habit; it's the kind of thing normal careful review already catches most of the time. The distinction matters because building habits around one-off noise wastes effort that should go toward the actual recurring cluster.

prompt: A coder's last fifteen corrections show three different error shapes: five combination-code misses, four specificity misses on musculoskeletal codes, and six unrelated one-off errors with no shared shape. Which cluster should she target first, and why?
hints: Which of these has the largest recurring count?
Do the six 'unrelated' errors actually form a cluster at all?
explanation: The combination-code misses (five) is the largest genuine recurring cluster with a consistent shape — worth a specific targeted fix. The specificity misses (four) are a real but smaller second cluster, worth targeting next. The six 'unrelated one-offs' aren't actually a cluster by definition — they don't share a shape, so there's no single habit change that would address all six at once; they're closer to normal background noise than a targetable pattern. Targeting the combination-code cluster first follows the module's own logic: fix the largest recurring, nameable shape first.

prompt: A double-coding mismatch just came back. Put these steps in the correct diagnostic order.

items: Read the note fresh, as if you'd never seen either coder's answer
Check whether the note clearly supports one reading over the other
If it clearly does, check whether one coder simply missed it (real error)
If the note doesn't contain enough information either way, treat it as documentation ambiguity, not a coder error

hints: The category test starts by setting aside who said what.
The last check is what separates true ambiguity from a real disagreement or a real miss.
explanation: Reading the note fresh matters first because it's the only way to classify honestly rather than defaulting to whichever coder sounds more confident. Checking whether the note clearly supports one answer comes next — if it does and someone missed it, that's a real error. If the note genuinely doesn't contain enough information for either reading, that's documentation ambiguity, and the fix is a clinician query, not correcting either coder.

prompt: In a double-coding adjudication, having both coders state their reasoning independently before either sees the other's rationale doesn't actually matter — the note's wording is what settles it either way.

config.statement: In a double-coding adjudication, having both coders state their reasoning independently before either sees the other's rationale doesn't actually matter — the note's wording is what settles it either way.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that seeing the other coder's rationale first can cause the second coder's stated reasoning to drift toward agreement, which would make it impossible to tell whether the mismatch reflected a genuine independent read or social pressure to align.

hints: What happens to the second coder's honesty about their own reasoning if they see the first coder's answer first?
Why would the order of stating reasoning matter if the note itself is the final arbiter?
explanation: False. While the note's wording is what ultimately settles the classification, the order still matters — if one coder's rationale is shared first, the second coder's explanation can drift toward agreement rather than reflecting an honest independent read, which makes it harder to tell whether a mismatch reflects real disagreement or just social pressure to align. Independent statements first preserve the diagnostic value of the mismatch itself.

prompt: A note reads: "Suspect early-stage renal insufficiency, nephrology referral placed, labs pending." What's the right coding approach?

options.text: Code confirmed renal insufficiency, since the clinical picture is strongly suggestive
Code only what's confirmed, or hold/query pending the labs — "suspect" signals the diagnosis isn't confirmed yet
Code it as ruled out, since nothing is confirmed

hints: What does "suspect" signal about diagnostic certainty?
Ruling something out and it being unconfirmed are two different things.
explanation: "Suspect" is hedge language, clinically and linguistically equivalent to "possible" — it signals the diagnosis is under investigation, not established. The honest approaches are coding only what's actually confirmed, holding the claim if pending results are expected soon, or querying the clinician. Coding it as confirmed overstates certainty the note doesn't contain; coding it as ruled out is equally wrong in the other direction — "suspect" and "pending" mean neither confirmed nor excluded.

prompt: Explain, in this module's terms, why putting an unconfirmed diagnosis into the record as if it were confirmed is a risk even when the guess later turns out to be correct.
hints: Who else reads a coded diagnosis besides the billing system?
explanation: The risk isn't really about whether the guess is right — it's about what a confirmed-looking code does in the record before it's actually confirmed. Other clinicians, future encounters, and risk-adjustment processes treat a coded diagnosis as an established fact, not a probability. Coding "suspected" as if it were "confirmed" exports false certainty into a record other people will rely on, regardless of whether this specific instance happens to be correct — the harm is in the false certainty itself, not in the eventual outcome.

prompt: A coder wants to fix her specificity-miss cluster on musculoskeletal codes. She decides her plan is 'pay more attention to laterality going forward.' Using this lesson's standard, what's missing from this plan, and rewrite it as something checkable?
hints: What three things does a real improvement plan need to name?
explanation: The plan as stated has no specific behavior (what exactly changes about how she reads a note), no defined sample (what claims will be checked), and no success criterion (what counts as it having worked). A checkable rewrite: 'Before finalizing any musculoskeletal injury code, explicitly check the note for a stated laterality (left/right/bilateral) and confirm the code includes it — checked against the next 20 musculoskeletal claims, with success meaning zero laterality misses in that sample and no increase in any other error type.'

prompt: If a targeted fix eliminates the originally-targeted error type completely, the improvement plan has definitely succeeded, full stop.

config.statement: If a targeted fix eliminates the originally-targeted error type completely, the improvement plan has definitely succeeded, full stop.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that the success criterion needs to also check whether any other error type increased as a side effect of the extra attention spent on the target — eliminating one error type while a different one quietly rises isn't a clean win.

hints: What's the second part of a complete success criterion, per this lesson?
Could fixing one thing cost attention somewhere else?
explanation: False. Eliminating the targeted error type is necessary but not sufficient — the lesson's full success criterion also checks whether any other error type increased, since the extra attention or time spent on the fix could crowd out attention elsewhere. A plan that only checks the targeted metric can miss a genuine net cost that a fuller criterion would catch.

prompt: A shop reports accuracy per-claim (any wrong code fails the whole claim). Which coder's number is most disadvantaged by this formula, all else equal?

options.text: A coder working single-code wellness visits
A coder working four-code inpatient claims
Formula choice doesn't disadvantage anyone

hints: Per-claim scoring punishes complexity — more codes on a claim means more chances for one to be wrong.
explanation: Per-claim scoring means a single wrong code among four fails the entire claim, exactly the same as if all four were wrong. A coder working complex multi-code claims has structurally more chances to trip that all-or-nothing threshold than someone working single-code visits, independent of actual per-code skill.

prompt: Order these steps for building an error profile from a list of recent corrections.

items: Read all recent corrections and assign each a specific error type
Count corrections by type to find the largest clusters
Re-check the largest cluster for hedge language that might mean ambiguity, not error
Build a targeted plan with behavior, sample, and success criterion for the confirmed largest cluster

hints: This mirrors the lab's own four stages.
explanation: Classification has to happen before counting, counting before identifying the largest cluster, and the ambiguity check has to happen before committing to a target — some of what looks like a coding error might actually be documentation ambiguity that a different fix (a clinician query habit) addresses, not a coding-behavior change.

prompt: A note says "COPD, resolved." Is this hedge language requiring an ambiguity classification?

options.text: Yes, "resolved" signals uncertainty
No — "resolved" is a confident, past-tense clinical statement, not a hedge
It depends on the coder's confidence level

hints: Compare "resolved" to "possible" or "suspect" — do they signal the same thing?
explanation: "Resolved" states a fact confidently — the condition existed and is no longer active. That's different from "possible" or "suspect," which signal the clinician hasn't yet reached a confirmed diagnosis. A mismatch involving "resolved" language is much more likely to be a real error or defensible disagreement than documentation ambiguity.

prompt: Two coders disagree on a claim. Coder A cites the note's exact wording for her code. Coder B says 'I just went with my gut, it felt right.' What does this asymmetry tell you about how to classify the mismatch?
hints: Does 'my gut' constitute a reading of the note's actual wording?
explanation: Coder A's answer is grounded in the note's actual text and can be checked against it directly. Coder B's answer isn't grounded in anything checkable — 'felt right' isn't a reading of the documentation, it's an unexamined guess. This asymmetry itself is diagnostic: it suggests Coder B's code may be a real error (not examined against the note at all) rather than a defensible disagreement, which requires an actual competing reading of the text, not just an impression.

prompt: A coder who consistently double-codes the same error type as a colleague, on the same charts, has probably found a real error rather than a personal habit.

config.statement: A coder who consistently double-codes the same error type as a colleague, on the same charts, has probably found a real error rather than a personal habit.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that when two independent coders converge on the same mistake on the same documentation, the note itself — not either coder's personal habit — is the more likely shared cause, worth investigating as a documentation or pipeline issue.

hints: If the same error shows up in two independent coders' work on the same charts, is it more likely to be a personal habit or something about the input itself?
explanation: True, with a caveat worth naming in the justification: two independent people converging on the same 'error' on the same documentation is a signal the cause may sit in the note or the pipeline's proposal, not in either individual's habits — worth investigating as a systemic issue rather than assigning it to one coder's error profile.

prompt: Which of these is the strongest evidence that an improvement plan actually worked?

options.text: The coder reports feeling more confident
The targeted error type dropped in the defined sample, with no other error type rising
The coder's overall accuracy number went up that month

hints: Overall accuracy can move for reasons unrelated to the specific fix.
What did the module say a complete success criterion checks?
explanation: A defined-sample, two-part check (targeted error down, no other error up) isolates the effect of the specific fix from noise and hidden trade-offs. Overall accuracy is too aggregated — it can move because of unrelated factors, and it wouldn't catch a hidden cost where the fix helped one thing while quietly hurting another.

prompt: A supervisor asks you to explain, in one sentence each, the difference between a real error, a defensible disagreement, and documentation ambiguity in double-coding.
hints: Each category needs a distinct test: what the note says, and how clearly it says it.
explanation: A real error: the note clearly supports one answer and a coder missed it. A defensible disagreement: the note genuinely supports either reading, and reasonable coders could land differently. Documentation ambiguity: the note doesn't contain enough information for either coder to know confidently, and the real fix is a clinician query, not picking a winner between the two coders.

prompt: A coder's accuracy dashboard shows 94% this month, 93% last month, 95% the month before — same formula throughout. What's the appropriate read?

options.text: A stable trend within normal noise, using a consistent, fair comparison
A concerning downward spiral requiring immediate intervention
The number is meaningless without knowing her colleagues' scores

hints: Same formula, same person, across time — is this exactly the comparison the lesson said is fair?
explanation: This is precisely the use case an accuracy rate is good for: one consistent formula, tracked over time, for the same person. A one-point wobble across three months reads as normal variation, not a spiral — and it doesn't need a cross-colleague comparison to be meaningful, since the fair, informative comparison here is against her own history.

prompt: Explain why a reviewer's last three items before hitting a target might be reviewed differently even though she objectively has enough time left for each one.
hints: What's competing with 'review correctly' as a goal in that moment?
explanation: The arithmetic being sufficient (five minutes per item) doesn't neutralize the psychological effect of a visible countdown against a visible target. As the target gets close, the countable goal (finish the remaining items) becomes more salient than the goal without a visible counter (catch every error), and attention narrows toward finishing rather than toward the specific checks each item needs — even though nothing about the actual time available has become insufficient.

prompt: Which metric would most plausibly reveal the end-of-day quality distortion this lesson describes?

options.text: Daily claims completed
A small monthly accuracy audit sample
An error-type analysis specifically targeted at claims completed in the last hour of the day

hints: Which metric directly rewards the distorted behavior, and which is too coarse to catch it?
explanation: Volume metrics directly reward the exact behavior in question (clearing items fast near a deadline), and a small monthly audit sample is disproportionately likely to miss the specific, harder judgment calls the distortion affects. Only an error analysis specifically targeted at the time window where the mechanism predicts distortion would actually surface it — which is exactly why the distortion can be real and invisible to standard reporting at once.

prompt: "The target feels unrealistic and I'm stressed" is a checkable claim a supervisor can act on.

config.statement: "The target feels unrealistic and I'm stressed" is a checkable claim a supervisor can act on.
config.rubric: A correct justification names what a checkable claim actually requires — a specific behavior, tracked evidence, and a bounded proposed change — and notes that a feeling, however real, gives the supervisor nothing to verify or act on.

hints: What are the three things a checkable claim names, per this lesson?
Can a supervisor verify or dispute a feeling the way they can verify a tracked behavior?
explanation: False. A feeling is real but not checkable — a supervisor has no way to verify, dispute, or act on it beyond a general reassurance. A checkable claim names the specific behavior the target produces, evidence that it's actually happening, and a specific proposed change — all three of which a feeling-based statement omits.

prompt: You suspect the target is causing you to skip specificity checks specifically on musculoskeletal claims late in the day. Design a two-week tracking plan to test this, naming what you'd log and why it targets the right window.
hints: What did the worked example's tracking plan target specifically, and why there rather than everywhere?
explanation: A strong plan logs, for each day, whether the specificity check (laterality, in this case) was explicitly run on musculoskeletal claims specifically in the last hour or last several items of the day, compared to earlier in the day. It targets that window because that's exactly where the end-of-period mechanism from lesson one predicts distortion — a flat log of all claims all day wouldn't isolate whether the effect is concentrated late in the day or spread evenly, which is the actual question being tested.

prompt: A coder's end-of-day recall consistently underestimates her time on harder items compared to system timestamps. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: She's deliberately lying to look more productive
Memory for effortful time is structurally biased toward compression, independent of intent
The system's timestamps must be miscalibrated

hints: Which explanation requires assuming bad intent, and which doesn't?
explanation: This gap is best explained by how memory for time-on-task actually works — effortful periods get compressed in retrospective recall, not by anyone deliberately misrepresenting their work. This matters because it points to fixing the tracking method (real-time or system-based logging) rather than assuming a character problem that a better method wouldn't actually solve.

prompt: Order these tracking methods from most to least reliable, per this lesson.

items: End-of-day recall from memory
A tally at natural breakpoints (end of each batch cluster)
A logged note at the moment you move to the next item
A system-generated timestamp

hints: Reliability tracks how close the recording happens to the actual event.
explanation: System timestamps are most reliable because they're not vulnerable to memory at all. Real-time item-transition notes are close behind, with only a seconds-long gap. Batch-cluster breakpoints introduce a modest gap (maybe twenty minutes) but stay reasonably reliable. End-of-day recall has the largest gap between the event and the recording, which is exactly where the drift discussed earlier in the module comes from.

prompt: Rewrite this into a functional accommodation request: "I have a condition that makes some days really hard and I need some kind of flexibility with my workload."
hints: Name what changes, what triggers it, and for how long — no diagnosis.
explanation: A functional rewrite names the operational shape without medical detail, for example: 'On days I flag by 9am, I need a reduced target of 25 items, with the remaining 15 made up over the following two days.' This specifies the trigger (a same-day flag), the change (a reduced number), and the resolution (made up over a defined window) — everything a supervisor needs to evaluate and implement the request, without requiring any diagnosis or symptom description.

prompt: A supervisor says "I need to understand what's actually going on before I can approve this." What's the best response, per this lesson?

options.text: Provide a full diagnosis to satisfy the request
Add more functional specificity — frequency, exact numbers, how make-up work is scheduled
Withdraw the request since it clearly needs more than a functional description

hints: Does 'what's actually going on' specifically request medical detail, or is that an assumption?
explanation: "What's actually going on" is ambiguous and can be answered honestly with more functional detail — how often flagged days happen, what the reduced target looks like operationally, how make-up work gets scheduled — without crossing into diagnosis. Treating any pushback as a demand for medical disclosure conflates 'explain more' with 'explain the diagnosis,' which aren't the same instruction.

prompt: Sort each item into whether it belongs in a personal work-decision record or not.

categories: Doesn't belong in the working record

items.text: The reasoning behind a close call on a specific claim, noted at the time
A general symptom diary unconnected to any specific work decision
items.category: Doesn't belong in the working record

items.text: A documentation gap flagged but unresolved before a claim was finalized
Real-time throughput and time-per-item notes

hints: The test is whether an entry documents a work decision or evidence relevant to a future work conversation.
General health tracking not tied to a specific work decision has a different, separate purpose.
explanation: The working record's scope is deliberately narrow: it holds reasoning, throughput, error patterns, and flagged gaps — things that document a specific work decision or serve a future work conversation. A general symptom diary, disconnected from any specific work decision, belongs in a personal health record instead — mixing the two doesn't serve either purpose well.

prompt: A coder wants to keep a thorough personal record but worries she won't sustain it. Using this lesson's approach, describe a version of the record that's realistic to maintain during a bad week.
hints: What three specific pieces did the lesson's lightweight system include, and roughly how much time did they cost?
explanation: A sustainable version layers onto habits already in place rather than adding a separate system: one-line notes at each item transition (the same habit as honest throughput tracking), a slightly longer note only on genuinely close calls (a few times a week, not every item), and a five-minute weekly skim to pull anything notable into the error-cluster or evidence documents. This totals around half an hour a week — small enough to survive a bad week, which is exactly when a heavier system would get abandoned.

prompt: Which of these is a checkable claim about a target, versus a feeling?

options.text: "I skip the secondary check on the last 3-4 items on 7 of the last 10 days"
"This target is just too much"
"I don't think this is fair"

hints: Which one names a specific, tracked behavior with a frequency?
explanation: Only the first option names a specific behavior, a frequency, and implies tracked evidence behind it — the other two are real feelings but give a supervisor nothing to verify or act on.

prompt: A coder's end-of-day log shows 4.0 min/item average; system timestamps show 5.1 min/item. What should she do about this gap before using either number in a conversation with her supervisor?
hints: Which number is method-biased, and which isn't?
explanation: She should use the system-timestamp figure (5.1 min/item), since end-of-day recall is structurally biased toward compressing effortful time, not the more reliable number. Bringing the inflated recall-based figure into an evidence-based conversation would undercut the very case she's trying to build, since it understates how much time the work actually takes.

prompt: Order the steps for building a checkable case that a target is unsafe.

items: Identify the specific suspected behavior and the window it happens in
Track that specific behavior with a method close to real time, over at least two weeks
Analyze whether the pattern is consistent or was one bad stretch
Draft a specific, bounded proposed change tied to the evidence

hints: This mirrors the lab's own stages.
explanation: Naming the specific suspected behavior and window comes first because it determines what to track. Tracking with a low-drift method over enough time distinguishes a real pattern from noise. Only after confirming a real pattern does a specific, evidence-tied proposal make sense — proposing a change before confirming the pattern exists would put the conclusion before the evidence.

prompt: An accommodation request that specifies a diagnosis will always be approved faster than a functional request without one.

config.statement: An accommodation request that specifies a diagnosis will always be approved faster than a functional request without one.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that a specific, bounded functional request is often easier and faster to evaluate precisely because there's less to interrogate — a diagnosis alone doesn't tell a supervisor what to actually implement.

hints: What does a supervisor actually need to evaluate a request — a diagnosis, or an operational description?
Which one gives a supervisor something concrete to simply approve?
explanation: False. A diagnosis doesn't by itself tell a supervisor what to implement — a bounded functional request (what changes, what triggers it, for how long) is often faster to evaluate and approve precisely because it's concrete and doesn't invite further probing questions the way a vaguer or more invasive disclosure can.

prompt: Name two things that belong in a personal working record and one thing that doesn't, per this module.
hints: The test is whether an entry documents a work decision or serves a future work conversation.
explanation: Belongs: real-time throughput/time-per-item data, and the reasoning behind a close call noted at the time it happened (or a flagged, unresolved documentation gap, or a named error cluster). Doesn't belong: general medical symptom tracking unconnected to a specific work decision — that serves a different purpose and belongs in a personal health record instead.

prompt: Why is a monthly accuracy audit unlikely to catch the end-of-day distortion this module describes, even if the distortion is real and ongoing?

options.text: It's too infrequent to matter
A small random sample is disproportionately likely to include the easier cases that survive the shortcut
Monthly audits only check Tier 1 items

hints: What kind of items does a small random sample tend to be full of?
explanation: A small monthly sample skews toward the easier cases across a queue, which are exactly the cases a rushed final stretch is less likely to get wrong. The audit passing isn't evidence the distortion isn't happening — it's evidence the sample hasn't yet caught the specific harder case where it would show up.

prompt: A colleague says "I just tell my supervisor everything about my condition so there's no confusion." What would you point out to her, using this module's terms?
hints: What does 'no confusion' actually require — full disclosure, or clear functional specificity?
explanation: Full disclosure isn't actually necessary to avoid confusion — a specific, bounded functional request (what changes, what triggers it, how long it lasts) is usually clearer to a supervisor than a diagnosis alone, since a diagnosis doesn't tell them what to implement. Full disclosure also isn't reversible once given, and most accommodation processes are entitled to functional information, not medical detail — so the extra disclosure isn't buying clarity it wouldn't otherwise have.

prompt: Match each tool to what it actually does.

pairs.right: Validates and helps assign individual codes against coding conventions
Takes a finished code set plus a few structured fields and outputs a DRG and its weight
Proposes candidate codes from the note's free text before a human ever sees them

right: A distractor: a different, unrelated tool description

hints: Think about the order these three tools actually run in.
Which tool needs a finished code set as its input?
explanation: These three tools run in sequence: the pipeline proposes candidate codes from the note, the encoder validates and helps finalize the code set against coding conventions, and the grouper takes that finished code set plus fields like discharge disposition to calculate a payment category. Each stage depends on the one before it being correct.

prompt: A DRG looks wrong on an inpatient claim. Walk through what a reviewer should actually check, in order, before escalating anything to IT.
hints: What are the specific inputs a grouper consumes, per this lesson?
explanation: First, check whether the code set fed into the grouper actually matches the documentation — a wrong or missing code is the most common real cause. Second, check the handful of structured fields the grouper also uses, especially discharge disposition and any present-on-admission or complication/comorbidity flags — these are exactly the kind of data-entry inputs that produce a plausible-looking but wrong DRG. Only after both of those check out clean is escalating to IT (to investigate the grouper software itself) a reasonable next step, since grouper software bugs are rare compared to input errors.

prompt: Explain why eleven open browser tabs creates more friction than a fixed set of three, even though eleven tabs technically holds more information available at once.
hints: What's the actual cost being minimized — available information, or search time on each switch?
explanation: The bottleneck this lesson identifies isn't how much information is available, it's how much cognitive re-orientation happens on every single switch between tools. Eleven similar-looking tabs means scanning and searching among them every time, which adds real, if individually small, friction across dozens of switches a day. A small, fixed, always-ordered set of tabs turns switching into muscle memory instead of a fresh search each time — the goal is fast, reliable switching, not maximum simultaneous information.

prompt: Order these steps for resuming a claim after an unplanned interruption.

items: Re-verify the specific pending item rather than trusting the note was complete
Check the scratch note for claim ID and status
Reopen the fixed tab set in its usual order
Navigate directly to the noted claim

hints: The scratch note has to be checked before anything else can be trusted.
The last step catches an incomplete note left mid-thought.
explanation: Checking the scratch note comes first because everything after depends on knowing where you actually were. Reopening the fixed tab set re-establishes the usual navigation pattern. Going directly to the noted claim avoids redoing finished work. Re-verifying the specific pending item, rather than trusting the note was complete, catches the case where the interruption happened mid-thought.

prompt: Sort each task by the best keyboard-first tool for it.

items.text: Scanning a long note for a specific medication name
Moving from the diagnosis field to the procedure field on a structured form
Jumping from the note to the encoder tab
Finding every mention of "denies" in a long discharge summary

hints: Match the tool to the type of navigation — searching text, moving through fields, or switching tools.
explanation: Find-in-page is built for locating specific text within one document. Tab order is built for moving through a structured form's fields in a logical sequence. A bound switching shortcut is built for jumping between separate tools or windows entirely. Using the right one for each task avoids the generic, slower fallback (visual scanning, mouse clicking, or cycling through everything with Alt+Tab).

prompt: Which of these genuinely resists a clean keyboard-only path in most review tools?

options.text: Typing a query note into a comment box
Freeform highlighting on a scanned, image-based document
Selecting a diagnosis code from a searchable dropdown

hints: Which interaction has no text or discrete list for a keyboard to navigate through?
explanation: Freeform annotation on a scanned image has no underlying text or discrete list structure for a keyboard to move through — it's a genuinely spatial task that needs pointer input of some kind. Text boxes are keyboard-native by default, and searchable dropdowns are usually well-supported (type to filter, arrows to move, Enter to select).

prompt: A coder notices she's looked up the same payer's documentation requirement for a specific procedure three times this month, each time taking about three minutes searching the manual. What should she do, and why does this specific case qualify?
hints: What's the test for whether something belongs in a personal reference?
explanation: It qualifies for the personal reference because it's already demonstrated recurrence — three times this month, not a one-off. She should add it to her personal reference the next time she needs it (or now, having noticed the pattern), which converts roughly nine minutes of lookup time this month, and more in future months, into a single quick check. The test isn't how hard any one lookup was, it's whether it's already recurred and is likely to keep recurring given her actual claim mix.

prompt: A personal reference, once built, should be treated as permanently accurate and never needs to be rechecked against the source material.

config.statement: A personal reference, once built, should be treated as permanently accurate and never needs to be rechecked against the source material.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that payer rules and coding guidelines change (e.g., annual guideline updates), and a stale reference that isn't periodically checked risks a fast wrong answer being trusted as much as a right one.

hints: Do payer rules or coding guidelines ever change?
What's worse — a slow right answer, or a fast wrong one?
explanation: False. Payer rules and coding guidelines do change, including routine annual updates, and a personal reference that's never revisited risks going stale — at which point it delivers a fast wrong answer with the same apparent confidence as a right one, which is worse than the slow lookup it replaced. A periodic (e.g., quarterly) skim to flag anything possibly outdated keeps the reference trustworthy.

prompt: Name the three pieces of hardware or setup choices this lesson identifies as most load-bearing for making reclined review work sustainable, and explain briefly why each matters more than it might first appear.
hints: Which three items did the evidence-stack activity mark as applicable?
explanation: An adjustable stand that holds the screen at eye level without hand support (without it, screen angle alone makes extended reclined work unsustainable); a separate, independently-positioned keyboard (a laptop's built-in keyboard forces a hand position tied to the screen, which a separate keyboard escapes); and voice-to-text for longer free-text entries (removes sustained typing entirely for exactly the tasks — escalation reports, query notes — where hand strain accumulates fastest). None of these are exotic, but each addresses a specific physical constraint reclined work introduces that an upright desk setup doesn't have.

prompt: On a bad-hands day, the right move for a genuinely hard drag-and-drop task with no button alternative is always to push through it reclined rather than delay it.

config.statement: On a bad-hands day, the right move for a genuinely hard drag-and-drop task with no button alternative is always to push through it reclined rather than delay it.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that forcing a hard spatial interaction through a worse ergonomic setup on an already-hard day compounds two costs at once, and that batching the task for a better-capacity moment is the more sustainable choice when no keyboard or button alternative exists.

hints: What did the queue-craft module say about stopping rules and not forcing work through on a bad day?
Does every task have to happen in this exact moment?
explanation: False. When no button-based alternative exists, forcing a genuinely hard spatial interaction through a reclined, worse-supported position on an already-difficult day compounds two costs — the task's inherent difficulty and the day's reduced capacity — rather than addressing either. The more sustainable move, consistent with the stopping-rule logic from the queue-craft module, is to batch that specific task for a better-capacity moment when it's realistic to do so.

prompt: A grouper output looks wrong, and a check confirms the code set and discharge disposition are both correct. What's the appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate to IT to investigate the grouper software itself
Assume the grouper is fine and ignore the discrepancy
Manually override the DRG based on a guess

hints: What does this lesson say to check first, and what's left once that's ruled out?
explanation: Once the inputs (code set, discharge disposition, and other structured fields) are confirmed correct, an IT escalation to check the grouper software itself is the reasonable next step — this is genuinely the rare case where the tool, not the input, may be at fault, but only after the far more common input-error explanation has been ruled out.

prompt: Describe, in one or two sentences, why a fixed three-tab navigation pattern is worth the upfront setup cost of learning it.
hints: What does the fixed pattern trade a small upfront cost for?
explanation: A fixed, always-ordered set of tabs turns tool-switching into muscle memory rather than a fresh visual search every time — the small upfront cost of learning a consistent pattern and its shortcut pays back across every single switch for the rest of a working day, which adds up to real time and cognitive-load savings compared to searching among a larger, unordered set.

prompt: Which lookup is the best candidate for a personal reference entry?

options.text: A rare diagnosis code looked up once for an unusual chart
A combination-code rule checked four times this month for a routine chronic-condition claim type
Every code definition ever looked up, to be safe

hints: What's the actual filter — difficulty, or demonstrated recurrence?
explanation: The combination-code rule has already demonstrated recurrence (four times this month) and is tied to a routine claim type likely to keep coming up — exactly what the reference is for. A one-off rare lookup doesn't earn a place even if it was hard, and caching everything defeats the reference's value by making it as slow to search as the original source.

prompt: A coder on a bad-hands day needs to do a task involving drag-and-drop reordering. What does this module suggest as the honest, sustainable move?
hints: Check for a button-based alternative first; if none exists, what's the other option?
explanation: First, check whether the tool actually has a button-based alternative to the drag-and-drop (many do, even when not obviously advertised) — that alone may solve it. If no such alternative exists, the honest move is to batch that specific task for a better-capacity moment rather than forcing a genuinely hard spatial interaction through a worse ergonomic setup on an already-hard day, which compounds two costs instead of addressing either.

prompt: A reclined workstation with a good stand, an independent keyboard, and voice-to-text eliminates all the ergonomic downsides of upright desk work.

config.statement: A reclined workstation with a good stand, an independent keyboard, and voice-to-text eliminates all the ergonomic downsides of upright desk work.
config.rubric: A correct justification names at least one genuine remaining gap — drag-and-drop, freeform image annotation, sustained precision mouse work, or video calls — that stays harder reclined regardless of the hardware setup.

hints: What did the second pod of the workstation lesson name as genuinely still hard?
explanation: False. Even a well-built reclined setup leaves genuine gaps: drag-and-drop interactions, freeform annotation on scanned images, sustained precision mouse work without stable arm support, and video calls all remain harder reclined than upright. The honest approach names these specifically and plans around them (a fallback tool, batching for a better moment) rather than claiming the setup solves everything.

prompt: Why is 'the specific laptop brand' not one of the load-bearing choices for a reclined workstation, per this module?

options.text: Brand doesn't determine the relevant features — adjustable brightness, screen finish, and size matter, and most brands offer comparable options
Laptop brand is actually the single most important factor
All laptops are functionally identical for this purpose

hints: What features actually matter, and are those brand-specific?
explanation: The features that matter (adjustable brightness, matte vs. glossy screen, size) aren't tied to a specific brand — most brands offer comparable options at this level, so the choice that actually drives usability is a stand, an independent keyboard, and voice input, not which company made the laptop.

prompt: A new coder asks you why they should bother learning Tab-key navigation through a form when clicking each field with the mouse 'works fine.' Give a one-paragraph answer using this module's reasoning.
hints: What's the actual cost being reduced — is it about speed, or about something else?
explanation: Clicking each field does technically work, the same way eleven open tabs technically works — the point isn't that the mouse method is broken, it's that Tab-key navigation removes a small, repeated physical reach-and-click that adds up across dozens of fields a day, every day, for someone managing a chronic condition where cumulative hand and shoulder strain is a real cost. It's the same logic as find-in-page and bound switching shortcuts: none of these are individually dramatic, but the payoff compounds specifically because they're used constantly, all day, every day.

prompt: A supervisor says "can you check the last quarter's telehealth claims, a couple of things seemed off." Turn this into a real scope statement using this lesson's three components.
hints: Population, trigger, and target-of-concern — what are each, specifically, here?
explanation: A real scope needs the population made specific (exactly how many telehealth claims, what date range), the trigger made specific (what were the 'couple of things' — get the actual claim numbers or issue types, not a vague memory), and the target named (is this about one telehealth-billing coder, one payer's telehealth rules, or telehealth claims generally). Without pinning down all three, the review can't be sampled or planned — it stays an open-ended hunch.

prompt: Explain why planning a batch review around an optimistic best-case daily volume (say, 50 claims a day, matching a routine queue day) risks reproducing a specific problem this phase already named.
hints: Which earlier module's mechanism specifically describes what happens when a plan runs out of time near its own deadline?
explanation: An optimistic plan that doesn't leave room for genuine full-depth review sets up exactly the end-of-period distortion the productivity module described: as the optimistic timeline runs out with items still left, attention narrows toward finishing rather than toward the specific checks the flagged claims actually need — the same mechanism, just triggered by a batch deadline instead of a daily target. Planning around a realistic pace, informed by the queue-craft module's actual pacing data, avoids setting up that same trap.

prompt: A batch review was triggered by three specific denied claims. Two sessions in, those three still haven't been reviewed. What does this module say about this situation?

options.text: It's fine, as long as overall volume is on track
The originating claims should have been prioritized and reviewed explicitly, ahead of the general triage system
The three original claims should be dropped from the review since the batch has moved on

hints: What's the actual reason this batch review exists?
explanation: The three original denials are the actual reason the batch review exists — letting the general triage system quietly deprioritize them just because overall volume looks good on track reproduces the exact metric-versus-goal distortion the productivity module named. They need explicit, early priority, not the default tier treatment.

prompt: Partway through a batch, a reviewer discovers the real shared dimension behind a cluster of errors is payer, not the specialty she originally batched by. Should she keep her original batching plan for consistency, or adjust it? Explain using this lesson's reasoning.
hints: Was the original batching plan a fixed rule or a starting hypothesis?
explanation: She should adjust it. The original specialty-based batching was a reasonable starting hypothesis about shared context, not a fixed procedure — and the standards-validation module already established that a surface label like specialty doesn't always track the dimension that actually matters. Once the data itself reveals payer as the real driver, re-sorting the remaining review around that dimension follows the same underlying principle the routine was built on; sticking to the original plan for its own sake would waste the discovery the sample review was for.

prompt: A reviewer finds 9 similar-looking errors out of 50 sampled claims. Name the two additional pieces of evidence this lesson says she needs before calling this a defensible systemic finding, and explain what each rules out.
hints: What did the evidence-stack activity mark as strengthening the raw count into a real finding?
explanation: She needs a comparison rate (the same error rate calculated for a relevant baseline group, such as other payers or other claim types) — without it, 9 out of 50 could just reflect that this group naturally has more of this claim type, not a genuinely elevated rate. She also needs a check on alternative explanations, such as whether the errors cluster after a specific date (supporting a timing-based cause) or concentrate among a few clinicians (suggesting an individual habit rather than a systemic issue) rather than spreading evenly — ruling out these alternatives is what separates a real systemic pattern from a coincidental cluster.

prompt: Rewrite this into a precisely worded finding: "There seems to be a coding problem with cardiology claims lately." Assume the actual data is: 7 of 38 sampled cardiology claims from Payer Y, submitted in the six weeks since a documentation memo went out, needed a diagnosis-specificity correction, versus 2 of 41 cardiology claims from other payers in the same window.
hints: Name the population, the rate, the comparison, and the timing — no more, no less.
explanation: "Cardiology claims submitted to Payer Y in the six weeks since [date of documentation memo] show a specificity-correction rate of roughly 18% (7 of 38), versus roughly 5% (2 of 41) for cardiology claims from other payers in the same window — consistent with clinician documentation not yet reflecting the memo's guidance for Payer Y specifically." This names the exact population, the rate with its comparison, the timing, and only the causal explanation the timing evidence actually supports.

prompt: Rewrite this escalation opening so a reader knows within one sentence what's being asked of them: "There have been some issues with orthopedics claims from a particular payer that might be worth looking into further at some point."
hints: Lead with the finding and the specific ask, per this lesson's structure.
explanation: A precise rewrite states the finding and the ask up front, for example: "Orthopedics claims to Payer X show a specificity-correction rate of 24% since March, versus 6% for other payers — requesting a clinician documentation-training session on Payer X's new requirement, to be scheduled by [name] within two weeks." This tells the reader immediately what was found, what's being asked, and of whom, rather than requiring them to read the full report just to find out whether it needs their action.

prompt: Sort each item by whether it belongs in the escalation report itself or the reviewer's own working record.

items.text: The precise finding statement with rate and comparison
The full 140-claim session-by-session log
A specific proposed action naming who should do what
An initial wrong hypothesis the reviewer tested and ruled out

hints: The test is whether a reader needs it to decide and act, or whether it's process detail.
explanation: The finding and the specific proposed action are exactly what a reader needs to decide and act quickly — they belong in the escalation. The full claim-by-claim log and the reviewer's ruled-out hypotheses are valuable process detail, worth keeping in the personal working record and available on request, but they'd bury the action-oriented structure if included in the report body itself.

prompt: A payer disputes a finding, claiming no documentation requirement changed. You have the payer's own dated policy update confirming it did. What's the right response, and why is this different from simply restating the finding more firmly?
hints: What does citing the specific document actually resolve that restating confidence doesn't?
explanation: The right response is sharing the specific, dated policy document directly, since it answers the payer's specific claim (that no change happened) with the actual evidence rather than with restated confidence. Restating the finding more firmly doesn't resolve anything, because the disagreement is about a checkable fact — whether the policy changed — not about how sure either side sounds. Producing the specific document that settles that fact is what makes the defense fast and conclusive instead of an unresolved standoff.

prompt: A clinician's challenge to one specific claim turns out to be correct — the reviewer missed a confirming statement later in the note. Beyond correcting that one claim, what else should the reviewer do, and why?
hints: What did the accuracy-measurement module say about a single error versus a recurring pattern?
explanation: Beyond correcting the specific claim, she should check whether the same fast-pass miss — reading only the first hedge-word mention without checking for a later confirming statement — shows up elsewhere in her sample, using the same error-cluster discipline from the accuracy-measurement module. A single missed claim might be a one-off, but if the pattern recurs, it's a real gap in her own review method that belongs in her personal error-cluster record and potentially affects the reliability of the larger finding, not something to fix in isolation and move past.

prompt: A batch review is prompted by "reimbursement seems lower than expected on recent inpatient stays." What's the missing scope component, per this module?

options.text: A specific target-of-concern — is this about one payer, one DRG family, or discharge coding generally
Nothing is missing — this is already a complete scope
The exact wording for the eventual escalation

hints: What does a real scope name that a general concern doesn't?
explanation: "Reimbursement seems lower than expected" doesn't yet specify what's actually driving the investigation — whether it's suspected to be one payer's rules, a DRG-family-specific issue, or general discharge-coding practice. Naming that target is what makes the rest of the scoping (population, trigger specifics) and the eventual sampling plan possible.

prompt: You find 4 similar-looking errors in a 60-claim sample, all from different clinicians, spread evenly across the sample period with no clustering. What does this specific evidence pattern suggest about the nature of the issue, if it's confirmed as a real pattern at all?
hints: Even spread across clinicians and time rules out which explanations?
explanation: Even spread across many clinicians and no time clustering rules out both a single clinician's habit and a specific triggering event (like a policy change on a given date) as the cause — if it's a real pattern at all rather than background noise, it would point toward something more general, like an ambiguous coding guideline or a systemic gap in the coding process itself, rather than a targeted, single-cause issue.

prompt: Which escalation opening is best structured per this module?

options.text: "Several things came up during this review, details below"
"Pediatric claims from Payer Z show a 19% specificity-error rate vs. 4% baseline since June — requesting a clinician documentation session by [date]"
A full table of all 80 reviewed claims, followed by a general summary

hints: Which option states the finding and the specific ask in one sentence?
explanation: The second option leads with the exact finding (rate, comparison, timing) and a specific, named ask — a reader knows within one sentence whether this needs their action. The other two either bury the finding in vague language or bury it under raw data the reader has to parse themselves.

prompt: A supervisor challenges your finding by saying "this just sounds like normal variation to me." What evidence from your finding would be the strongest direct response, and why?
hints: What's the one number that distinguishes 'normal variation' from a real elevated rate?
explanation: The comparison rate against a relevant baseline is the strongest direct response — "normal variation" is exactly the claim a comparison rate is built to test. If the flagged group's rate is meaningfully higher than the baseline group's rate in the same sample, that's direct evidence against the variation explanation; if it turns out the two rates are actually close, that's a sign the supervisor's challenge might be right and the finding needs revisiting.

prompt: If a challenge to a finding turns out to be wrong, the right response is to restate the original finding as forcefully as possible.

config.statement: If a challenge to a finding turns out to be wrong, the right response is to restate the original finding as forcefully as possible.
config.rubric: A correct justification notes that the right response is producing the specific evidence that answers the specific challenge, not simply restating confidence — evidence resolves a factual disagreement in a way that forcefulness doesn't.

hints: What actually resolves a disagreement about a checkable fact?
explanation: False. Even when a challenge turns out to be wrong, the right response is the specific evidence that answers it directly — a dated document, a comparison rate, whatever resolves the actual factual disagreement — not simply restating the finding with more confidence. Forcefulness doesn't settle a checkable disagreement; the underlying evidence does.

prompt: A reviewer wraps up a capstone-style batch review and finds no defensible pattern in her sample. Is this a failed review? Explain using this module's terms.
hints: What did the lab explicitly say about a no-pattern outcome?
explanation: No — an honest conclusion that no defensible pattern emerged from a properly scoped and sampled review is a legitimate, valid outcome, not a failure. The value of the review process is in the rigor of the scoping, sampling, and evidence standard applied, not in guaranteeing a dramatic finding — forcing a pattern that the evidence doesn't actually support to avoid an 'empty' result would be a worse outcome than an honest null finding.

prompt: Name the one thing that has to be true about a reviewer's working notes for her to be able to write a fast, evidence-based defense when a finding is challenged weeks later.
hints: What connects the honest-tracking module to the defense skill in this one?
explanation: The reviewer's own record from the review process — the specific claims sampled, the specific evidence for the pattern, the dated source documents — has to actually exist and be specific enough to retrieve quickly, rather than relying on memory weeks after the fact. This is the direct payoff of the personal working-record habit built earlier in this phase: a defense built on a well-kept record is fast and specific; a defense built on memory is neither.
